client: I’ve been really anxious about the family reunion next month. Ever since the argument with my cousin last year, I can’t stop thinking about how awkward it’s going to be. I’m not sure therapy can help with this—it feels like there’s no way to avoid the tension, and I don’t know if talking about it will change anything.
therapist: It sounds like this upcoming reunion is weighing heavily on your mind, especially with the unresolved tension from last year. I hear some uncertainty about whether therapy can help, and I’m curious—what would it look like if things *did* feel a bit more manageable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess if things felt more manageable, I wouldn’t be dreading it so much. Maybe I’d feel like I could handle whatever happens, even if it’s awkward. But I don’t know how to get there—it’s not like I can control how my cousin acts or what they say. That’s what makes me feel so stuck.
therapist: It sounds like you’re really focusing on what’s outside your control—like your cousin’s actions—and that’s understandably leaving you feeling stuck. What if we shifted our focus to what *is* within your control, like how you might prepare yourself emotionally for the reunion?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess I could try to prepare emotionally, but I don’t even know where to start. Every time I think about it, my mind just goes in circles about what could go wrong. I feel like no matter how much I prepare, I’ll still end up feeling overwhelmed and anxious when I’m actually there.
therapist: It sounds like your thoughts are getting caught in a loop of anticipating the worst, which can be overwhelming. I notice you’re speaking quickly—it seems like this topic really stirs up a lot of energy. What do you think might help slow those racing thoughts down, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think slowing down my thoughts would help, but it’s hard to do when I’m so worked up. I’ve tried breathing exercises before, but they don’t always work for me—I feel like I’m just going through the motions without actually calming down. Maybe there’s something else I could try, but I’m not sure what would really make a difference.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling a bit stuck between wanting to slow your thoughts and not finding the breathing exercises as helpful as you’d hoped. What’s it been like for you when you try those exercises—what’s going through your mind at that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I try breathing exercises, I usually end up thinking, “Am I doing this right? Is this even helping?” It feels like I’m just waiting for something to happen, but I don’t feel any calmer. I guess I get frustrated because it feels like I’m putting in effort but not getting the result I want.
therapist: It sounds like frustration is creeping in when the breathing exercises don’t feel as effective as you’d hoped, especially when you’re already feeling worked up. What if we explored a different approach—something that feels more natural or engaging to you in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I’m open to trying something different, but I’m not sure what would feel natural. When I’m anxious, it’s hard to focus on anything—it’s like my brain is racing, and I can’t settle on one thing. Maybe there’s an approach that doesn’t feel so forced, but I don’t know what that would look like.
therapist: It sounds like you’re looking for something that doesn’t feel forced or overly structured, especially when your mind is racing. What if we explored grounding techniques that feel a bit more intuitive, like focusing on physical sensations or engaging your senses in a way that feels natural to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Focusing on physical sensations might help, but I’m not sure how to do that when I’m in the middle of a family reunion. It feels like I’d just be distracted the whole time, and I don’t want to seem disengaged or rude. I guess I’m worried that trying to ground myself would make me feel even more disconnected from everyone around me.
therapist: It sounds like you’re worried that grounding yourself might make you feel more disconnected or come across as rude, which adds another layer of concern. What if we explored subtle ways to stay present—things that could feel natural and help you stay engaged with the moment without drawing attention?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Subtle ways might work better, but I'm still not sure how to do that without it feeling forced. Like, if I focus on the taste of food or the feeling of my drink in my hand, what if I just end up hyperfocusing on that instead of the conversation? I feel like I can't win - either I'm anxious or I'm distracted.
therapist: I hear the frustration in your voice as you describe feeling trapped between anxiety and distraction—it’s like no option feels quite right. Let’s think together: what’s one small moment from a past gathering where you felt *somewhat* at ease, even if just briefly? Sometimes those moments hold clues about what works.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess there was one time last year when I was talking to my aunt about her garden. She was really passionate about it, and I found myself getting interested in what she was saying. For a little while, I wasn’t thinking about the awkwardness or worrying about what my cousin might do. But I don’t know if that’s something I can recreate—it felt like it just happened naturally.
therapist: It sounds like that conversation with your aunt felt like a brief but meaningful escape from the tension—almost like a natural anchor in the moment. What do you think it was about that interaction that helped you feel more at ease? Was it the topic, the way she spoke, or something else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think it helped because she was so genuinely excited about her plants—it was easy to get caught up in her enthusiasm. But I don’t know how many people at the reunion will be like that, and I can’t exactly ask my aunt to only talk about gardening all night. It feels like that moment was just luck, not something I can really plan around.
therapist: I notice your voice brightened when you described that moment with your aunt—it seems like her genuine enthusiasm really lifted your mood, even if just temporarily. Rather than trying to recreate that exact scenario, what if we explored how you might seek out or create more of those lighter, engaging moments at the reunion?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
